articles.title: ‘Lanterns’ Finale: Hal Jordan’s Killer and Manhunter Revealed, Sinestro Creates [SPOILER], John Stewart Powers Up for ‘Superman’ Sequel
articles.summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the “Lanterns” finale, now streaming on HBO Max. Have no fear, the “Lanterns” finale is here. The season finale — or possibly the series finale, since HBO hasn’t renewed the show yet — wrapped up the mystery posed by the show’s premiere of who…
body: In present day, back on the planet decimated by the Manhunters, John interrogates Sinestro (Ulrich Thomsen) and learns that Noah freed the villain from prison. Sinestro reveals that he harnessed the fear-inducing gas from the planet to create a new, yellow ring for Noah. As comics fans know, Sinestro is the creator of the Yellow Lanterns, an evil group opposed to the Green Lanterns who derive their power from fear. Sinestro offers John the chance to charge his depleted ring from the sinister, yellow lantern, but Hal’s hologram stops him, and they leave Sinestro marooned on the planet.

Noah ambushes John when he returns to Earth, the two drive back to Rushville together. Noah reveals that he didn’t burn down Hal’s house, but says he was the one who killed him. He claims he couldn’t let Hal reveal his identity as a Manhunter and the yellow lantern to Kerry. Noah says he’s trying to overcome his violent Manhunter programming, and asks that John kills him to protect everyone from what he might do. John doesn’t answer, but lets Noah go and play one last football game for Rushville.

articles.title: Korean Directors Rally Behind ‘The Assassin(s)’ as Political Firestorm Turns on Its Makers
articles.summary: The Directors Guild of Korea (DGK) has come out in support of the team behind “The Assassin(s),” Hur Jin-ho’s thriller about the 1974 shooting of first lady Yuk Young-soo, as political anger over the Korean box office leader spills onto its cast and crew.
body: The guild said the hostility had moved past questioning the film’s content and its makers’ choices, and “is targeting the daily lives and livelihoods of those who took part, and has gone as far as demanding that such a film never be made again.”
The statement, which named neither Hur nor anyone else, accepted that every film attracts harsh reviews along with praise, and asked who could draw an exact line between fair and excessive criticism.
“Creators can be criticized for their work, but that criticism must not lead to the collapse of the creator’s personal life and livelihood,” the guild said.

The DGK added that its idea of a healthy creative environment includes standing beside filmmakers who want to begin again, because “the chance for that person to start their next story should not disappear simply because a film went through controversy and criticism.”

articles.title: Korea Box Office: ‘The Assassin(s)’ Holds Admissions Lead as ‘Chiikawa’ Generates Top Weekend Gross
articles.summary: Director Hur Jin-ho’s political crime thriller “The Assassin(s)” held the top position at the South Korean box office in admissions over the weekend of Oct. 2–4, though Japanese animated feature “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” captured the frame’s largest gross revenue.
body: “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” launched wide on Sep. 30 following limited festival previews. Directed by Kei Oikawa and adapted from the manga by Nagano, the animated fantasy adventure follows the titular character and friends traveling to an island haven before confronting a mysterious aquatic legend. Counting nationwide previews, the anime has grossed $4.7 million from 604,764 total admissions.

Gambling crime drama “Tazza: The Song of Beelzebub” placed third in its sophomore frame, taking in $2.2 million from 299,915 admissions across 1,093 screens for an 18% market share. Directed by Choi Kook-hee and starring Byun Yo-han, Noh Jae-won, and Ayaka Miyoshi, the fourth installment in the comic-adapted franchise has grossed $10.2 million from 1,365,648 viewers since its Sep. 23 rollout.

“ The Odyssey ” took fourth place in its ninth frame, drawing $1.2 million from 123,059 admissions across 678 screens. Its local gross reached $101.2 million from 11,998,236 ticket buyers, leaving the film just under 2,000 admissions shy of the 12-million-ticket threshold.

articles.title: J. Todd Anderson, ‘The Nice Guys’ Storyboard Artist and Longtime Coen Brothers Collaborator, Dies at 67
articles.summary: J. Todd Anderson, the storyboard artist behind films like “The Nice Guys” and “Raising Arizona” and a longtime Coen Brothers collaborator, has died following a battle with cancer. He was 67. His death was confirmed in a Facebook post on Oct.
body: Anderson first began his work as a storyboard artist in the late 1980s with the Joel and Ethan Coen-written comedy “Raising Arizona.” From there on out, Anderson remained a frequent collaborator with the Coen Brothers, going on to storyboard each of their films. This included “Miller’s Crossing,” “Fargo,” “The Big Lebowski,” “The Ladykillers,” “True Grit,” “Hail, Caesar!” and “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” in addition to their solo projects like “Drive-Away Dolls” and “Honey Don’t” from Ethan and “The Tragedy of Macbeth” from Joel.

Beyond the Coen Brothers, he is credited with having worked on 1989’s “Twister,” 1991’s “The Addams Family,” 2009’s “Whip It,” 2018’s “The Predator,” and 2016’s “The Nice Guys.” Over his career, he was nominated for three Art Directors Guild awards for “The Tragedy of Macbeth,” “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” and “Hail, Caesar!” He also directed 1999’s “The Naked Man” and 2008’s “My Mummy.”
Born John Todd Anderson in Springfield, Ohio, he later attended Wright State University. The Tom Hanks Center for Motion Pictures at the university shared a tribute to Anderson on Facebook.

articles.title: Marshals Season 2 Addresses Kayce's Controversial Reaction To John Dutton's Death
articles.summary: Yellowstone fans have often debated Kayce's reaction to John Dutton's death, and the Marshals Season 2 premiere suggests Kayce is also conflicted about it.
body: "Marshals" is continuing the trend of calling back to various "Yellowstone" moments. In the Season 2 premiere, "All Hat No Cattle," Kayce Dutton (Luke Grimes) sets out to retrieve his son from Tom Weaver (Chris Mulkey). In the process, he's willing to trade his family for vengeance in an echo of a controversial "Yellowstone" Season 5 plot point that seems to bother Kayce as much as it does fans.

John Dutton's death in "Yellowstone" Season 5 was controversial, to say the least. Fans simply weren't ready for Kevin Costner's towering neo-Western figurehead to be killed off-screen in a death that bore all the trademarks of a hasty re-write following creator Taylor Sheridan and Costner's well-publicized behind-the-scenes clashes. Amazingly, Sheridan then proceeded to follow up this contentious death with another divisive development — namely, having Kayce track down the gunman responsible for his father's demise, only to let the guy go.

articles.title: Kit Harington Addresses the Devastating ‘A Tale of Two Cities’ Finale and Its “Horrific” Impact
articles.summary: Kit Harington discusses A Tale of Two Cities, the love triangle at the core of the classic story, and joining the Harry Potter series for Season 2.
body: Editor's note: The following contains major spoilers for A Tale of Two Cities.

In the finale of the MGM+ series A Tale of Two Cities, entitled “Resurrection Man,” Sydney Carton ( Kit Harington ) made the heartbreaking decision to sacrifice himself so that the one he loved could have the family that would have otherwise been impossible. After Charles Darnay ( François Civil ) is arrested in Paris at the height of the Revolution and his trial uncovers shocking revelations that tear him away from Lucie Manette ( Mirren Mack ) and sentences him to death, Sydney realizes that he’s going to have to take matters into his own hands to stop it.

After watching the season of this classic adaptatio n, Collider got the opportunity to chat with Harington about the key to making it relatable now, fleshing out the characters, exploring the love story between Sydney and Lucie, Sydney’s heartbreaking self-destruction, his decision to trade places with Charles in the finale, and what it was like to work with a guillotine. He also discussed joining the Harry Potter TV series in Season 2, and how he feels about the final season of Industry.

articles.title: Why George Russell From The Gilded Age Looks So Familiar
articles.summary: If you recognize the man who plays George Russell on The Gilded Age but can't quite put your finger on where you've seen him before, we've got you covered.
body: HBO has made many great shows over the years — so many, in fact, that it's easy for some to slip through the cracks. Not that these shows receive no love, but they perhaps don't get brought up as often as something like "The Sopranos" or "Game of Thrones." One ongoing historical drama that started in 2022 fits the bill. "The Gilded Age" is HBO's glitzy period drama where class conflict reigns supreme. It features an impressive cast, including one Mr. Morgan Spector as George Russell. He has a certain air of familiarity to him, and for good reason.

The show chronicles the conflict between old and new money in New York City's glittering Gilded Age. Season 1 kicks off in 1882 and centers on Marian Brook (Louisa Jacobson), an orphaned daughter of a Union general who moves in with her old money aunts and gets caught up in the lives of her stupendously rich neighbors. Season 2 picks up in 1883 by focusing on Bertha (Carrie Coon), who sets out to challenge the old guard by backing the new Metropolitan Opera House, while George (Spector) faces his own battles at his largest steel plant.

articles.title: Zoe Kazan on Honoring Steinbeck’s ‘East of Eden’ for Netflix Series While Rethinking Its Characters
articles.summary: The series creator explains her decision to build the adaptation around a love story, between brothers, rereading Cathy Ames and how she updated Steinbeck's novel for television.
body: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’ s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.
When Zoe Kazan was working on adapting John Steinbeck’s acclaimed novel East of Eden, she recalls being asked the same question: Why not begin with Cathy?

“She interrupts this love story,” Kazan tells The Hollywood Reporter, “and if we don’t establish that love story to start between these two brothers, we don’t understand the stakes of her interrupting it.”

That realization became one of many while crafting a series on a book that spans 50 years and stretches across the country but that Kazan insists is built on the characters, rather than spectacle. She told every department head, from costumes to hair, that the work of their show would succeed only if audiences left talking about the characters.
points: The series creator explains her decision to build the adaptation around a love story, between brothers, rereading Cathy Ames and how she updated Steinbeck's novel for television.

articles.title: ‘Lanterns’ Team Breaks Down Finale’s Emotional Gamble, Hal Jordan’s Ultimate Fate and John Stewart’s Future
articles.summary: Some viewers might take issue with one major swing, but the team sees it as "remixing" rather than "rewriting" Green Lantern canon.
body: For a Lanterns season one finale that ends with John Stewart taking flight as his own brand of Green Lantern, it’s a rightfully grounded affair until then.

“There was never a version of the finale that was more action-oriented,” Lanterns showrunner Chris Mundy told moderator Mallory Rubin of The Ringer during the finale press conference, which featured the creative brain trust alongside stars Pierre and Chandler. “If we landed it emotionally with [Hal and John], we would’ve done our job. [Action for action’s sake] would’ve been distraction and incident instead of emotion.”
Structurally, co-creator Damon Lindelof considers episode five’s “Battle of Rushville” to be this series’ version of the CGI slugfest and sky-beam invasion we’ve seen time and time again.

“If we had to make a two-hour Lanterns movie, you would have to have a bombastic third-act action set piece — and then two or three minutes of coda,” Lindelof said. “We got to do that [coda] over the course of [the last] three episodes.”

articles.title: Marshals Season 2 Premiere Ending Twist Explained: Who Really Killed Garrett
articles.summary: The Marshals Season 2 premiere tells us who killed Kayce's former Navy SEAL squad mate Garrett Garvey, played by Riley Green.
body: "Marshals" Season 1 was a strange collection of episodes that oscillated between taut crime thriller, family drama, and action series, all within a regrettable network procedural framework. One week it looked as though we'd be getting a show about Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton covering up his family's crimes while simultaneously forging a new law enforcement career. The next, it seemed Kayce and Tate Dutton's (Brecken Merrill) grief at losing Kelsey Asbille's Monica Dutton would be the main focus. Then, Double-G showed up.

Country songster Riley Green played Kayce's former Navy SEAL squad mate Garrett Garvey on a show that seemed to revel in weaving new story threads while struggling to figure out which of its existing threads to follow. Double-G, as Logan Marshall-Green's Pete Calvin called him, was a troubled man — a haunted badass with the soul of an artist who just wanted to play his songs and forget about the fact that, as we eventually discovered, he was essentially responsible for the death of his, Kayce, and Pete's other SEAL teammate, "Roner." Then, disaster struck.
